## When a coordinate stays constant {#fv3-constant-coordinate .fv-lesson .line-lesson}

```{=html}
<p>Revisit Example 3.1:</p><div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="\underset{\sim}{r}=(1+\lambda)\underset{\sim}{i}+(1-\lambda)\underset{\sim}{j}+\underset{\sim}{k}"></span></div><div class="line-constant-layout"><div><div data-line-constant></div><p class="line-graph-caption">The line lies in the plane <span data-math="z=1"></span>.</p></div><div><div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="x=1+\lambda,\qquad y=1-\lambda"></span></div><div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="z=1"></span></div><p>Eliminate <span data-math="\lambda"></span> from the changing coordinates:</p><div class="fv-equation"><span data-math="\boxed{x+y=2,\qquad z=1}"></span></div><p>Keep the constant coordinate as a separate equation.</p></div></div>
```

<div class="booklet-cue">Booklet Example 3.1 and §3.2.1 · pp. 39, 42</div>

::: {.notes}
A fixed axonometric diagram shows the line x+y=2 lying in the plane z=1, one unit above the xy-plane. The sample points (0,2,1), (1,1,1) and (2,0,1) all have height 1. The zero k component of the direction vector leaves z unchanged. The plane patch illustrates part of an infinite plane; it is not a bounded region. Both x+y=2 and z=1 are needed. Never divide by the zero direction component.
:::
